newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa lists seven for $1 bln Telkom sale.
newsitem.headline: South Africa lists seven for $1 bln Telkom sale.

text.p: The South African government on Thursday shortlisted seven international telecommunications concerns as candidates to take a stake of over $1 billion in state utility Telkom.

Post and Telecommunications Minister Jay Naidoo said the companies from Europe, the United States and the Far East would carry out a due diligence investigation into Telkom's financial and technical resources.

The government is offering a 20-30 percent stake in the telecommunications group to foreign firms as the first major step in a privatisation programme seen as a litmus test of its commitment to economic reform.
A further 10 percent will be offered to black economic empowerment groups.
The firms shortlisted are Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom, KPN of the the Netherlands, Telekom Malaysia, South Western Bell of the United States, Italy's Stet and Telia of Sweden.

Bell Atlantic Corp had withdrawn following its link-up with Nynex while British Telecommunications, also listed as a prospective partner, was only interested in niche market possibilities, Naidoo said.

Postmaster General Andile Ngcaba said the government expected to raise some five to six billion rand ($1.1-1.3 billion) in cash from the sale of a 30 percent stake in Telkom, plus additional investment in technology and training.
"Five to six billion rand is the cash component. The value could go to seven billion," he told reporters.

Telkom needs 30 billion rand in the next five years to double the number of telephone lines from four million serving mainly white areas at present to eight million, with a much greater penetration of traditionally black areas.
Half of that amount is expected to come from Telkom's own revenue with the balance from borrowings and cash from the strategic equity partner.
"We need the most modern technology. That is one important element of delivering affordable telephony," Naidoo said.
The cabinet has resolved to conclude the equity partnership deal by next April.

Naidoo said there were no preferred bidders and his ministry would encourage the formation of consortia between parties of complementary strength. Shortlisted companies would be able to introduce other partners, subject to them meeting ministry critera, he added.

Several variables remained up for negotiation which would influence the final price paid by a privatisation partner. These included the length of exclusivity granted to Telkom under its licence, which Naidoo said was likely to be around five years.

Economists are looking anxiously at the Telkom deal, both for its ability to boost government coffers and as an indication of the readiness of President Nelson Mandela's government to push through market-friendly policies.

Other state enterprises which could follow Telkom down the road to full or partial privatisation include South African Airways, the Airports Company, sections of the rail and road transport network, state-owned leisure facilities and, possibly, electricity generator Eskom.
